title: Notification service
prompt: Design a notification service that other teams' services call to reach users by push, email and SMS. It sends 500 million notifications a day, and marketing campaigns burst to 50,000 a second. Users choose which kinds of notification they get on which channel, and quiet hours in their own time zone. Security codes must arrive within 10 seconds; marketing can wait minutes. Delivery goes through third-party providers (APNs, FCM, an email provider, an SMS provider) with their own rate limits and outages, and nobody should receive the same notification twice.
explanation: Most of the work is outside your control: providers throttle, fail and get retried. What it tests is keeping urgent messages away from bulk traffic with separate queues, honouring preferences, and getting delivery that looks exactly-once from parts that are at-least-once.

requirements: Separates channels, user preferences, quiet hours and priority levels
Gives different delivery targets for transactional messages (seconds) and marketing (minutes)
Makes no duplicates and a delivery status per notification explicit requirements
estimation: About 5,800 notifications a second on average (500 million ÷ 86,400), with bursts of 50,000
A delivery log of about 250 GB a day at roughly 500 bytes a notification, several terabytes for a month
api_data_model: A send call taking user, template, data, priority and an idempotency key, returning a notification id
Tables for preferences and device tokens, templates, and a delivery log with a status per channel
Uses the idempotency key to ignore a repeated send from a caller that retried
architecture: An API that validates and enqueues, then workers that apply preferences, render templates and call providers
Separate queues per priority and per channel, so a campaign cannot delay security codes
Looks up preferences, quiet hours and device tokens before fanning out to channels
scalability: Queues absorb campaign bursts and workers drain them at the rate the providers accept
Throttles each provider to its limits and scales workers for each channel independently
Partitions queues by user id so one user's notifications stay in order
reliability: Retries with exponential backoff and parks notifications that keep failing in a dead-letter queue
Dedupes on the notification id or idempotency key so a retry is not delivered twice
Fails over to a second provider when one is down, and drops a security code that has expired rather than send it late
communication: Follows one security code from the calling service to the user's phone
Explains how the design stops marketing bursts from delaying urgent messages
